name: Executive order of April 27, 1876 restoring the western part of the White Mountain reservation to the public domain
nations: Cibecue and Southern Tonto Apache groups (Western Apache, as named in Docket 22-D)
promises: Not a treaty: a presidential order. It restored to the public domain all the White Mountain reservation lying west of a line from the northwest corner of the reserve (on the southern edge of the Black mesas, due north of Sombrero or Plumoso butte) south to that butte, southeast to Chromo peak, south to the mouth of the San Pedro river and due south to the reservation's southern boundary (Royce p. 884, area 592).

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission concluded that by the executive orders of August 5, 1873, July 21, 1874, April 27, 1876, January 26, 1877, March 31, 1877 and December 22, 1902 the United States successively extinguished, without paying compensation, Western Apache Indian title to lands inside the enlarged White Mountain reservation, as of the dates of the orders. The order of April 27, 1876 is one of the orders it named.

landTaken: Royce area 592: the White Mountain reservation west of the line Royce describes. The Commission did not reach the acreage because the claim was settled.
compensation: None at the time. The Western Apache claim (Docket 22-D) was compromised for $4,900,000 in 1972, for all the Western Apache lands taken.
today: The Fort Apache (White Mountain) and San Carlos reservations remain.

openQuestions: This tract (area 592) is not mapped on any other record, and the Commission names this order; it is counted as its own taking, as cession-1877-03-31-apache is for area 602.
Whether all of area 592 lay inside the Western Apache title area of Finding 11 was not plotted; the per-tract acreage and value were never found because the claim was settled.
The order's own text was read only in Royce's summary.

Audit 2026-11-08: reopened OSU 932 (conclusion 5 names April 27, 1876; quote exact), OSU 1611 and OSU 1055 ($4,900,000). Royce p. 884 text (Sombrero or Plumoso butte, Chromo peak, mouth of the San Pedro) matches. Double-count check: area 592 is mapped only here, not on cession-1871-11-09-apache (541, 573, 582, 603), cession-1877-03-31-apache (602, 603) or cession-1886-10-01-apache-western-bands (689, land outside the reservation, conclusion 4). Conclusion 5 and the order that follows it call for a separate acreage and value per excluded tract and date, so this is a distinct taking; no sameEventAs.

plain.promised: Not a treaty: a presidential order. It cut the western part of the White Mountain reservation, west of a line through Chromo peak to the mouth of the San Pedro, out of the reservation.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found in 1969 that by this order and others the United States took Western Apache land inside the reservation without paying for it.
plain.today: The Western Apache claim was settled for $4,900,000 in 1972, for all their lands taken. The Fort Apache and San Carlos reservations remain.
